analytic.title: Work-In-Progress: Simplifying CPS Development with Real-Time Virtual Resources

div.p: The specification, design, prototyping, analysis, implementation, information management, verification, privacy and security guarantees, safety assurance, and maintenance of cyberphysical systems (CPS) are extremely complex, owing to the multitude of operating systems, software components, hardware platforms, communication infrastructures, sensors and activators, human-machine interfaces, and numerous intertwined feedback loops. This paper describes a project to simplify all these life-cycle phases of developing and maintaining CPS by introducing Real-Time Virtual Resources (RTVR). RTVR forms a virtual layer between application software components and physical resources consisting of hardware platforms, communication infrastructures, and sensors and activators so that the software components can be implemented without knowledge of the details of the physical resources and thus can be ported from one physical resource into another with ease. Such open systems make it easy to add and remove software applications and reduce implementation cost when compared to systems which physically assign distinct computing resources to run different applications. However, most existing virtualization schemes [2, 13] significantly under-utilize the underlying physical resources in order to maintain the schedulability of real-time tasks as if they were scheduled on dedicated physical resources. Also, these schemes are not transparent to the software applications in that they need to be aware of each other and modification of the software may be necessary. Our proposed RTVR based on the Regularitybased Resource Partition (RRP) Model [7,9] overcomes the above shortcomings, making it a true contender in simplifying all phases of CPS development and maintenance. This paper outlines the first of four project tasks to be performed: the specification, design, prototyping, analysis, implementation, verification, and maintenance of CPS with RTVR. 564 2019 IEEE Real-Time Systems Symposium (RTSS)

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Consider for instance the scheduling of component tasks in the specification, design, prototyping, implementation, analysis, and verification of a Cyber-Physical System (CPS) [4,16]. Traditional scheduling focuses on one or a "stand-alone" set of resources (such as the CPU, a multi-core processor, or a network router) while in a CPS, the scheduling of tasks (both physical and computer-based) of physical elements consisting of a multitude of sensors and actuators interconnected to the computing and communication substrates must be holistically determined and analyzed. For example, the start of task executions in a processor may depend on the availability of inputs from sensors that are transmitted via wireless links between the sensors and the processor. Processing times within the sensors, end-to-end link transmission delay, and tasks in the processors must be analyzed together to determine a correct task schedule. This complex collection of systems, tasks, and resources require new design practices and a paradigm that facilitates scheduling that can provide real-time and reliability guarantees. The current approach of directly mapping and executing application tasks on physical resources such as processors or cores running a variety of operating systems (OS) further exacerbate the problem of analysis, verification, correct implementation, interoperability, and maintenance.

Real-Time Virtual Resources (RTVR): With the goal of integrating multiple real-time applications onto a single physical platform, Hierarchical Real-Time Scheduling (HiRTS) allows different real-time applications to share space or time on a computational resource in [7,8] by mapping different applications to distinct Real-Time Virtual Resources (RTVR) running on physical platform(s). However, our recent work has not considered HiRTS and RTVR in the context of CPS, hence here we explore the potential for RTVR to significantly simplify the development and maintenance of CPS. Resource sharing improves efficiency, and is one of the reasons for the increasing popularity of open and cooperative systems. Compared to systems where we physically assign distinct computation resources to run different applications, open systems make it easy to add or remove applications, increasing resource utilization and reducing implementation cost. In a CPS, there are even strong incentives for openness and cooperation in the communication and computational aspects. Even more important, having a uniform virtual resource layer between applications and the underlying physical computation and communication elements means that these applications need not be aware of the physical resources' details and vice versa. There are multiple advantages with the use of RTVR. First, it facilitates interoperability and porting of an application from one physical platform into another. Second, it simplifies the specification, design, prototyping, analysis, implementation, verification, and maintenance of CPS because there is uniform virtual layer between applications and physical resources, avoiding the complexity of modeling and implementing applications running directly on different physical platforms. Third, it enhances information management as well as privacy and security since applications are isolated from one another in their virtual resources or containers. Finally, it can potentially lead to safer, more fault-tolerant CPS components since fault tolerance can be handled by the virtual layer while applications need not introduce extra fault-tolerance measures, as shown by our preliminary work [5,6].

Virtualization technology [22][23][24] has become increasingly popular. We first describe how to share time on one computation resource based on a practical 2-layer HiRTS system (Figure 1). Other physical resources such as communication elements (like routers and switches), sensors, and even actuators can be virtualized. A computational resource could be a single resource or an identical multiresource (i.e., identical computing elements such as multi-core processors) and it is temporally divided into a group of resource partitions (i.e., intervals of available times on this resource), which are managed by a global resource-level scheduler. On each resource partition, the real-time tasks belonging to a real-time application is scheduled by its own task-level scheduler. The resource partition is an intermediate layer in this 2-layer system, and each resource partition only uses the computational resource for only a fraction of the time. HiRTS has several resource models. Typically, each HiRTS model has its own definition of resource partition containing some parameters. For example, in the Periodic Model [12], a resource partition exactly obtains c computation time units in each period p.

A time unit (also called time slice or time slot by other researchers) is a system-defined unit of time for the purpose of scheduling, and there is no (either partition or task) preemption in it. Therefore, we may assume that all time parameters such as task periods and deadlines are integers without loss of generality. The parameter values of a resource partition are collectively called its signature. For example, periodic partition (10; 4) represents a partition which obtains 4 time units in each period of 10 time units. The signature of a resource partition is the only information shared between the global resource-level scheduler and its own task-level scheduler. The resource-level scheduler gathers all the partition signatures in the system and decides how to assign time units to the partitions. We call this the resource partitioning problem in HiRTS. Meanwhile, on each resource partition, real-time tasks are usually migrated from a non-hierarchical real-time system where they were directly running on a dedicated computation resource under a specific scheduling policy, such as Earliest Deadline First (EDF) or Rate Monotonic (RM) [10]. In most cases, the original schedulability tests for a dedicated resource do not work for a resource partition which only preempts a fraction of the computation time. Therefore, new task scheduling techniques are needed. We call this the task scheduling problem in HiRTS. Now, we start to address the relevant problems.

At the resource level, a basic problem is how to schedule partitions on a single resource. In the multiresource case, there are two dominating categories of scheduling algorithms: global scheduling and partitioned scheduling. Global scheduling allows resource partitions to migrate between different computation resource units, while partitioned scheduling does not. They may dominate each other depending on different resource models (a resource model specifies how a hardware component such as a core or CPU is temporally allocated to higher-layer virtual resources). Therefore, when considering the resource partitioning problem, we need to investigate both global scheduling and partitioned scheduling.

For task scheduling, one model we consider is the Periodic Task Model, in which two successive requests of each task are separated by exactly the same time interval, called its period. In this model, a task t i is denoted by (c i ; p i ; d i ; o i ), where c i , p i , d i and o i are its execution time, period, deadline and offset, respectively. Most current HiRTS Models have investigated a simple case of the Periodic Task Model, in which each task's deadline is same as its period and offset is 0. Another considered task model is the Sporadic Task Model, in which two successive requests of a task are separated by at least a time interval, called its minimum separation time.

Simplifying the Specification, Design, Prototyping, Analysis, Implementation, Verification, and Maintenance of CPS with RTVR: Having a uniform RTVR virtual layer between applications and physical resources simplifies the specification, design, prototyping, analysis, implementation, verification, and maintenance of CPS. Consider specification and verification: if applications run directly on different physical resources with a multitude of operating systems and runtime platforms, these OS's and platforms must each be specified, modeled, and verified. Their interactions, which must then be specified, modeled, and verified, are far more complex than that of having a single uniform virtual layer. Formal models for CPS should capture the following four characteristics [18]: (1) discrete-time behavior of the computational elements; (2) continuous dynamics of the physical environment (plant); (3) spatio-temporal variation of the continuous physical parameters; and (4) aggregate effects resulting from concurrent operations of networked computational elements. There is a variety of techniques and tools for specification, modeling, and verification. We have used Real-Time logic (RTL), which is capable of specifying discrete or discretized timing constraints of CPS. We have discovered the most expressive RTL subset called Linear RTL [1] which contains polynomial-time-analyzable RTL formulas.

We have successfully used RTL to specify the timing behaviors of embedded systems including a nuclear power plant controller of the moveable control rods [19], the Boeing 777 Integrated Airplane Information Management System [20], and the prototype ISS X-38 Crew Return Vehicle autonomous spacecraft avionics [3,11], and then to efficiently verify the satisfaction of the required timing and safety properties. The challenge is to scale-up and extend RTL-based verification to CPS. This project will demonstrate that specifying, modeling, and verifying CPS employing RTVR will be significantly easier (shorter time and space exploration) than non-RTVR CPS. Also, we will extend our RTL-based optimization approach to optimize and synthesize CPS components and the CPS as a whole in the design/specification phase since 70-80% of a product's (CPS here) cost is determined by the decisions made in this phase [21].

Clean Separation and Transparent Task Scheduling: Our preliminary experiments via simulation show that the Regularity-based Model outperforms the Periodic Model in terms of allowable maximum utilization of the hardware resources. Furthermore, considering that the Regularity-based Model is able to handle comprehensive task models at the task level, it should be a better choice than the Periodic Model when integrating real-time applications, especially in a complex CPS. This owes to the fact that in the Periodic Model, task scheduling on resource partitions with EDF (earliest deadline first) or DM (deadline monotonic) requires the development of new utilization bounds and complicates design whereas in the Regularity-based Model, the existing and proven utilization bounds remain unchanged. This project aims to apply the concept of Real-Time Virtual Resources (RTVR) and Hierarchical Real-Time Scheduling (HiRTS), several versions of which have been evaluated via highly abstract task models where many tasks are treated as a single schedulable unit, and analyze the former in the context of a CPS. With HiRTS, a computation resource is divided into a group of temporal resource partitions called Virtual Resources (VR), each of which accommodates multiple realtime tasks. In particular, our Regularity-based Resource Partition (RRP) Model achieves the highest transparency in task scheduling, thus minimizing the interface coupling and improve the interoperability of both new and legacy components. As a result, this scheduling framework potentially facilitates the integration of multiple applications in the computational and communication space of a CPS.

Our vision is to enhance the HiRTS/RTVR framework to schedule and run context-aware tasks in computational and communication elements of a CPS. Currently, Virtual Resources are computation elements such as CPU's and cores. This project will develop the theory of Virtual Resources to communication and physical CPS elements. The proposed project is to demonstrate and validate this scheduling framework utilizing an efficient modeling and verification environment to be built.

With our proposed hierarchical scheduling and virtual resources framework, each task set in a CPS component, or example, an autonomous vehicle's control unit can be mapped to its virtual CPU. New task sets with additional functionalities can request virtual CPU's while old tasks with functionalities that are no longer needed can release their CPU's without affecting the scheduling and execution of other virtual CPUs' task sets. This significantly facilitates scheduling and isolates task sets from one another, leading to better fault isolation and easier verification.

div.head: II. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: The project will evaluate the efficacy of RTVR via a simulated CPS followed by a small-scale real CPS. One test CPS application is our city-wide traffic CPS [16,17,27] which aims to balance a city's traffic among its roads and reduce travel time for each vehicle. We have obtained promising results for an individual vehicle [17] and our next step is to develop multi-vehicle cooperation. Here we describe more details of the traffic CPS for Real-Time Traffic Routing (RTTR) by collaborating vehicles in a congested city area. Without Real-Time Virtual Resources, the CPS consists of many vehicles, network infrastructures, satellites, sensors, and other components running software components directly on these physical resources, often with different operating systems. This project will investigate the introduction of the RTVR layer so that all software tasks run on these virtual resources which are connected uniformly to the underlying physical resources.

The RTTR system observes traffic situation in the area and sends routing instructions to each vehicle, in order to optimize an overall throughput metric. The system's response time is designed to meet real-time requirements of the domain. Each vehicle (conventional, semi-autonomous, or autonomous) receives routing instructions from the Real-Time Learning and Decision System (RTLDS) which observes traffic situation in the area and analyzes historical as well as predicted traffic flows in order to optimize one or more metrics. These metrics include travel times for all vehicles from their starting points to their respective destinations. Note that this is not a selfish system since it is not optimizing the travel time of a single vehicle but the average travel time of all vehicles while balancing the traffic among all the roads in the congested area. The system's response time is designed to meet realtime requirements of the domain.

This RTTR system can be useful now to participating vehicles and becomes important in the future when cars are connected. Our plan is to start developing the systems for a small area and then scale it to larger areas in the future. A typical traffic-flow simulator [26] simulates traffic on freeways and arterial networks. It takes as input the road topologies and geometries or other traffic characteristics as well as real-time traffic measurements from a network of traffic detectors such as cameras or loops. The system uses a mathematical traffic flow model to perform traffic-flow simulation and predict the traffic conditions in real time.

In the future where vehicles are wireless-connected, each car's position can be sent to the RTTR system in real time, thus increasing the accuracy of the system. This collection and processing of real-time vehicular data, the periodic execution of the traffic-flow simulator, and periodic guidance to each vehicle must meet stringent timing constraints for the routing guidance to be useful. In addition to being an engineering problem of mathematical modeling of the traffic flow, the RTTR system must learn from real-time data to provide more accurate routing guidance. These data may also include nontraffic-related information such as each driver's lunch and dinner schedules and locations, which can be used to further increase the predictive power of the RTTR by letting it know in advance where the cars are headed in the near future.
